p: Amos uses a rare word, noqed, that may mean a man who raised sheep in numbers.
b: The Hebrew is noqedim, not the usual ro'im "shepherds" (compare 1:2). The only other use is for King Mesha of Moab, a noqed who paid Israel a tribute of lambs and wool (2 Kings 3:4). An Ugaritic text uses a related title for a chief herdsman of a temple. Some scholars conclude that Amos managed or owned flocks and was no poor hired hand (Hayes, Andersen and Freedman); others keep "shepherd" for the lower rank (Wolff). The Greek does not translate the word: it writes it as a name, "Akkarim".

t: Tekoa: a Judean preaching in the north
p: Tekoa was a village in the hills of Judah, about ten miles south of Jerusalem.
b: Amos came from Judah but his words are aimed at the northern kingdom (1:1, 7:12-15). Tekoa stood on the edge of the wilderness of Judah, good for grazing but poor for crops. Later Tekoa is known as a place that could raise a warning alarm (Jeremiah 6:1) and as the home of the wise woman who spoke to David (2 Samuel 14:1-20). Because the book goes to Bethel, Samaria and the northern shrines, many readers treat Amos as a foreigner who crossed the border to speak. Others think he may have sold his wool and figs at northern markets.

p: The Hebrew says the words were seen, not heard.
b: The verb is chazah, "to see", the root of chozeh, "seer" (7:12). A prophet can "see" a word (Isaiah 2:1; Micah 1:1), and the same verb opens Isaiah's book (Isaiah 1:1). The title does not say whether Amos means visions or only that the word came to him with the force of something seen. The five visions of 7:1-9:4 are called "showing" (hir'ah), a different verb, but they certainly belong to this sense.

p: A great earthquake was remembered for centuries; the date is uncertain.
b: Zechariah later says people fled "as you fled from the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah" (Zechariah 14:5, own rendering from the Leningrad Codex). The earthquake dates the book, not the other way round: Uzziah and Jeroboam II overlap from about 790 to 753 BC, so the book falls somewhere in the middle of the 8th century. Yigael Yadin tied a destruction layer at Hazor (Stratum VI) to this earthquake, and a 2000 study by Austin, Franz and Frost argued from Dead Sea sediments and other sites for a very large quake near 750 BC. Neither match is accepted by everyone. Pottery dating is only accurate within decades and an earthquake leaves no name; the dating of the Hazor layer is itself disputed; and the lead author of the 2000 study works for a young-earth research institute, so his thesis of a very large quake is treated with caution. Jewish tradition tied the quake to the day King Uzziah went into the Temple to burn incense and was struck with skin disease (2 Chronicles 26:16-21): Rashi, Radak and Ibn Ezra all mention it, and Ibn Ezra adds that Scripture gives no proof, only tradition.

p: Jeroboam II ruled Israel for 41 years; Uzziah ruled Judah for 52.
b: 2 Kings 14:23-29 tells of Jeroboam II in only a few verses: he "won back Israel's border, from Lebo-hamath to the Sea of the Arabah" (2 Kings 14:25). This was the northern kingdom's greatest size and wealth since Solomon, helped by the weakness of Aram (Damascus) and the quiet of Assyria in these years. The same period is told from Judah's side in 2 Chronicles 26. Amos shows what that prosperity looked like to the poor. The Plain English Translation says "Uzziah" as in 2 Chronicles; 2 Kings calls him Azariah.

p: The motto of the book is a lion image that returns at 3:4, 8; the same words open Joel 3:16.
b: The roar of a lion is a sign of attack on prey (3:4, 8). The same line stands in Joel 3:16, and in Hosea 11:10 the LORD "roars" to call his children home. Scholars debate which text used which. One view is that Joel quotes Amos; another that an editor placed the motto in both books to tie the Twelve together (Nogalski, Schart). In Hebrew the two lines are the same words (yitten qolo), and the Plain English Translation gives them the same English in Amos 1:2 and Joel 3:16. Zion is where the LORD lives, while Amos speaks in the north at Bethel, so the motto puts the LORD's voice in Judah's capital; Wolff and Jeremias think a Judean editor placed it at the head of the book. Jewish commentators read it in other ways. Rashi says the speech goes out "from the Holy of Holies". Radak says the roar and the voice are a figure for prophecy, as in 3:8. Ibn Ezra offers a great thunder that will hold back the rain, or a voice the prophet heard. The Targum drops the lion: "The LORD said ... from Jerusalem he will lift up his word."

p: Carmel was known for lush growth, so its withering shows the force of the roar.
b: Mount Carmel on the coast is among the wettest and greenest heights in Israel (Isaiah 35:2; Song of Songs 7:5). When the LORD roars, the shepherds' meadows in the dry south and the greenest summit in the north are alike scorched. The verse covers the whole land from the wilderness to the sea. Amos comes back to the mountain at 9:3, where it is no hiding place.

a: For three rebellions of Damascus, and for four
p: A number pattern with a surprise: three, and then more. Each nation is charged with one crime.
b: The pattern "a number, and the next number" is a Hebrew way to say "enough, and more than enough": three and four in Proverbs 30:15, 18, 21, 29 and Sirach 26:5, six and seven in Job 5:19, seven and eight in Micah 5:5, nine and ten in Sirach 25:7. The sayings in Proverbs 30 name three and then four things, and the fourth is the point. In Amos the numbers are not counted: each nation gets one named crime. The Hebrew word pesha' is "rebellion", a breach of trust between a lord and a vassal (the Plain English Translation uses "rebellion" throughout; compare 1 Kings 12:19). The ruler is the LORD, and the rebellion against him is shown in how they treat other people.

a: I will not turn it back
p: The Hebrew has no object: the verb is shuv, "to turn back", and it is not said what is turned.
b: lo ashivenu has a pronoun "it" that has no antecedent. It may be the punishment, the decision, the word or the anger. "Revoke it" (many English Bibles) chooses punishment or decision. Medieval Jewish commentators and modern ones choose one of these. The Plain English Translation keeps the verb that means "turn back" and leaves the object open, as in the Hebrew. Compare 4:6, where Israel does not "turn back" to the LORD, and 9:14.

p: Aram under Hazael crushed Israelite territory east of the Jordan.
b: A threshing sledge was a heavy board with iron or stone teeth dragged over grain. To "thresh" a people was a picture for brutal conquest (Isaiah 41:15; Habakkuk 3:12). Hazael king of Aram took Gilead and the land east of the Jordan from Israel (2 Kings 10:32-33) and then pressed Israel under Jehoahaz (2 Kings 13:3-7), because the king of Aram "had destroyed them and made them like dust to be trampled" (2 Kings 13:7). The Hebrew word behind "trampled" is the one for threshing (dush), the same root as the threshing of Gilead here. The event is from about 840-800 BC, a generation or two before Amos. The Plain English Translation's "citadels" is the term used also in Jeremiah 49:27; see 1:4.

a: fire into the house of Hazael
t: Fire on the walls: a refrain
p: Seven times the same punishment comes: fire on the walls and citadels (1:4-2:5).
b: Each oracle against a foreign nation or Judah has the same punishment: "I will send a fire". The line "it will eat up the citadels of Ben-hadad" matches Jeremiah 49:27 word for word in the Hebrew ("I will light a fire in the wall of Damascus, / and it will eat up the citadels of Ben-hadad", Jeremiah 49:27). Whichever way the borrowing went, the image is fixed by Amos 1-2 and used again by Jeremiah and others. Hazael and Ben-hadad are the two Aramean kings of 2 Kings 13:3, father and son.

a: those who live in the Valley of Aven
t: "The one who lives" or "the one who sits"?
p: The Hebrew word means "one who sits or lives", and it may mean a ruler seated on a throne.
b: yoshev is plain "inhabitant", but it is paired with "the one who holds the scepter", which suggests the same kind of person: a ruler "sitting" in the Valley of Aven and in Beth-eden. Aven means "wickedness" or "nothing" (compare 5:5, where Bethel will become Aven). It may be the Beqa' valley in Lebanon, near Baalbek. Beth-eden may be Bit-Adini, an Aramean state on the Euphrates. All of this is guesswork, the identification is not certain. Kir (see 9:7) is the place the Arameans came from and now return to.

p: Philistine cities took captives and sold them to Edom, far to the south.
b: galut shelema is a "complete exile": a whole population carried off. The charge is of slave trading, not war (Joel 3:6 and Ezekiel 27:13 name the same trade). Edom had to be a buyer, since it lay along the caravan routes to Arabia. Gaza stands for the Philistine cities (1:8). Because there is no known raid of this size in the 8th century, some date the verse earlier, to the time of Jehoram of Judah (2 Chronicles 21:16-17), while others think of a raid from Uzziah's day. The Plain English Translation keeps "communities" for the word shelema, "whole".

p: Gath is missing from the list.
b: The Philistines had five cities (Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Ekron, Gath). Amos names four. Gath may be left out because Uzziah had broken its wall (2 Chronicles 26:6) or because Hazael had already destroyed it (2 Kings 12:17), which would date the list after that event. Yet Amos 6:2 still speaks of "Philistine Gath", so the question stays open. Some also note that Amos 9:7 includes the Philistines among the peoples the LORD guides. "Remnant" here is the ordinary word she'erit; see 5:15.

p: Tyre broke a treaty "of brothers", probably with Israel.
b: Hiram of Tyre called Solomon "my brother" and made a treaty with him (1 Kings 5:12; 1 Kings 9:13). Many read the covenant as that old treaty between Tyre and Israel, which Tyre broke by selling Israelite captives to Edom. Others think "brothers" means Edom itself (since Edom and Israel are brothers by Jacob and Esau, Genesis 25:23) or a general treaty of kindred peoples. The oracle has no mention of Israel by name, so the reference is uncertain.

t: Edom and Israel: Esau and Jacob
p: Edom is charged with unrelenting hostility to a kinsman.
b: Edom is Esau, and the "brother" is Israel (or Judah). The two peoples were in constant conflict: Edom refused Israel passage (Numbers 20:14-21), revolted from Judah under Jehoram (2 Kings 8:20-22) and was a long-term enemy (Obadiah 10-14; Ezekiel 25:12-14; Lamentations 4:21-22). The charge here is a sin against kinship: the verb "destroyed his compassion" uses rachamim, the word for the love between family members (Genesis 43:30). "His anger tore on and on" has the Hebrew yitrof, the verb for a beast that tears its prey (Hosea 6:1; Amos 3:4 uses the noun teref, "prey").

t: Ammon and the pregnant women of Gilead
p: A brutal crime of war, done to enlarge territory.
b: Ripping open pregnant women is a crime of conquest named elsewhere (2 Kings 8:12; 2 Kings 15:16; Hosea 13:16). The aim is to wipe out a people at the root, so that the land they held would be empty. The Ammonites claimed Gilead as their own at times (Judges 11:12-28; Jeremiah 49:1). Amos's list of Gilead's wrongs (Damascus 1:3, Ammon here) shows how often the land east of the Jordan was crushed. The Plain English Translation says "their own land" to bring out the Hebrew "so as to enlarge their territory".

a: burned the bones of the king of Edom into lime
t: Moab and the bones of Edom's king
p: Moab burned a king's bones for plaster, a crime against the dead.
b: The deed is not recorded elsewhere in the Bible; 2 Kings 3:26-27 mentions Moab's king and the king of Edom in battle, but not burning bones. To burn bones to lime was to deny a king his tomb and his rest (compare 2 Kings 23:16, where Josiah burns bones on an altar). The shame of the dead mattered in the ancient world. Note that Moab is not charged with a crime against Israel: the oracles are against wrongs among nations, which the LORD judges. This is a key point in the structure of chapters 1-2, as the eighth oracle, against Israel, will show (2:6). Rashi and the Targum say the king's bones were burned and the lime was spread on the walls of a house as an insult. Radak ties the crime to 2 Kings 3:27 and reads the son offered there as the Edomite king's son; Ibn Ezra gives the same link as one view.

t: Judah: a different kind of charge
p: Judah's sin is against the LORD's teaching, and not like the sins of the other nations.
b: The charge against Judah uses torah, "teaching", and chuqqim, "rules" (the Plain English Translation follows the site's wording; see the term list). It is the only one of the eight without a named cruelty. Many critical scholars (Wolff, Jeremias) think 2:4-5 was added by a Judean editor, in the Deuteronomic style (Deuteronomy 4:5-8; 2 Kings 17:19), because it does not give a deed and because it is worded like the editors of Kings. Others (Paul, Andersen and Freedman) defend it as Amos's own: a prophet from Judah would name his own people. The oracle does hold the listeners' attention: it brings the series near to Israel.

p: The word for lies, kazav, may mean idols, as the Greek reads it.
b: kizvehem is "their lies". The Greek has "their vain things", and the word is used for false gods (Psalm 40:4; compare Jeremiah 16:19-20, "lies ... worthless things"). Many take it to mean idols or false teaching, and the ancestors "walked after" them like followers of a master. If so, the lies are what the prophets and priests said (Jeremiah 23:25-26). The Plain English Translation keeps "lies".

t: Selling the poor for a pair of sandals
p: A person sold into debt slavery for a tiny sum.
b: The "righteous" here is the one who is in the right in a lawsuit and the "needy" is the poor man who cannot repay (see 8:6 for the same picture). The picture is debt slavery: a person who could not pay a small debt was sold to work it off (Exodus 21:2-11; 2 Kings 4:1; Nehemiah 5:1-5). A pair of sandals may be the amount of the debt or a symbol of its smallness; it may also point to a land transaction, since a sandal was handed over to seal a sale (Ruth 4:7-8; Deuteronomy 25:9-10). Which of these is meant is debated. The law said to treat a bonded Israelite as a hired worker and set him free in the seventh year (Leviticus 25:39-43; Deuteronomy 15:12-15).

a: push the humble off their road
t: Pushing the humble off the road
p: The Hebrew says "turn aside the way": it may mean pushing them out of the way, or twisting their case.
b: derekh "way" can mean the road a person walks or his path in life. "Turn aside the way of the afflicted" may mean to force the humble off the path in the street, or to bend a case in court, as the same verb is used of denying justice (Exodus 23:6; Isaiah 10:2; Amos 5:12). The Plain English Translation's picture of a shove at the roadside leaves both open. The verb "trample" in the first line (sha'ap) can also mean "pant after", and the Greek has a different verb ("they strike the heads of the poor"). The verse is hard in the Hebrew.

a: go in to the same young woman
t: The father and son and the young woman
p: The Hebrew leaves the woman's status open; the crime is exploitation, which may or may not be incest.
b: na'arah is a "young woman" or "girl", often a servant. The text does not say she is a wife. Readings: (1) a slave girl abused by both father and son, against the slave laws (Exodus 21:7-11); (2) a woman used in the shrine, a cult-prostitute (compare Hosea 4:14); (3) a daughter-in-law, which would be incest (Leviticus 18:15; 20:12). Many ancient and medieval readers took her as a servant used by both. The next words, "so that they profane my holy name", fit any of the three, because sexual abuse of the helpless turns the LORD's name into something ordinary (Leviticus 18:21; 20:3).

p: The law said to give a poor person's coat back by sundown.
b: The Torah allowed a loan secured by a coat but told the lender: "give it back to him by sundown" (Exodus 22:26), "because it is his only covering, the cloak for his skin" (Exodus 22:27). The same is in Deuteronomy 24:12-13: "Be sure to give the pledge back to him at sundown, so that he can sleep in his coat" (Deuteronomy 24:13). Amos shows the rich keeping the coats and using them as bedding at the altar, a double wrong: they break a law about the poor and use the proceeds to worship.

p: The wine was bought with money taken from fined debtors.
b: yein 'anushim is "wine of the fined": wine bought with fines taken from those who could not pay, or taken as payment (compare Exodus 21:22, where the same root names a fine). The priests, or the wealthy at the shrine meals, drank it in "the house of their God". The Hebrew is plural-looking elohehem, which can be "their God" or "their gods"; the Greek has "their God". The charge is theft turned into worship.

t: The Amorites in the story of Israel
p: The LORD reminds Israel of the conquest and the exodus.
b: The Amorites stand for the people of Canaan, the tall people of Numbers 13:28-33 and Deuteronomy 2:10-11, 21. The images of cedar and oak describe strength, and "fruit above and roots below" is a way to say "totally" (compare Ezekiel 17:9; Malachi 4:1). In 2:9-12 the LORD lists what he did: the conquest, the exodus, the wilderness, the prophets and Nazirites. These are all gifts he gave Israel, and Israel's response is 2:12.

p: Nazirites were people set apart by a vow, like Samson, and Amos puts them next to prophets.
b: A Nazirite vowed to avoid wine, to let the hair grow and to keep clear of the dead (Numbers 6:1-21). Samson (Judges 13:5-7) was a Nazirite from birth. Samuel's mother vowed that no razor would touch his head (1 Samuel 1:11); the Hebrew does not use the word Nazirite, but Mishnah Nazir 9:5 and a Dead Sea scroll of Samuel (4QSam-a) do. Amos says the LORD raised them up as signs of holiness: prophets speak God's word, Nazirites live as a picture of holiness. Israel made the Nazirites break their vow by giving them wine and commanded the prophets not to speak (2:12). Both show the same attitude: Israel wanted its holy people to be silent or to be like everyone else.

a: press you down where you stand
p: The verb me'iq is rare; the Greek has "I will roll".
b: me'iq from the root 'uq occurs as a verb only here. Proposed senses: "press down" (a cart pressing the ground under its load), "groan" (the cart creaking, with the people), "make totter", "cut" or "split". The Greek has "I will roll under you, as a cart rolls full of straw." Some see a harvest image: the ground gives way under the full cart of sheaves. The Plain English Translation takes the pressing sense and reads it as the LORD crushing his people under their own weight. All the senses end in the same disaster.

a: run away naked on that day
p: One scroll has a different word for "brave".
b: The Masoretic Text has ve-amits libbo, "strong of heart". The transcription of 4Q78 (4QXIIc) reads u-motse libbo where the Masoretic Text has amits; the sense is not clear, and it may be a scribal slip. 4Q82 (4QXIIg) preserves the line with amits in brackets (restored). The Plain English Translation follows the Masoretic Text. I cite the Abegg-Bowley-Cook transcription of the scrolls, and the official editions are in DJD XV (Ulrich and others, 1997).

p: Amos speaks to both kingdoms in 3:1 and calls them one family.
b: mishpachah is the clan or family. "The whole clan that I brought up from the land of Egypt" takes in all the tribes, north and south. The exodus is the LORD's first act toward the people, and this sentence sets up the argument of 3:2: those he rescued are responsible to him. Amos's "against you" ('aleikhem) puts the listeners in the dock before the next verse begins.

a: You are the only ones I have known
t: "You are the only ones I have known": election and responsibility
p: The verse joins the LORD's choice of Israel with a harder duty.
b: yada', "know", is used of the LORD's choice of Abraham (Genesis 18:19), of Israel in Egypt (Hosea 13:5) and of Jeremiah before birth (Jeremiah 1:5); it means personal commitment. Most commentators agree that Amos does not deny Israel's election but says it brings more accountability, not less (Wolff, Paul). The verse turns the people's comfort upside down. Christian traditions read the verse differently on what "known" means for the Church and for salvation; see the card on the chapter page. A common Jewish and Christian reading is that to be chosen is to be held to a higher standard. Rashi takes "know" as "love" (I loved you, and you rebelled) and points to the Talmud (Avodah Zarah 4a); Radak and Ibn Ezra compare a king who is angrier at the servants who stand before him than at strangers.

t: Punish, visit, or call to account?
p: The Hebrew verb paqad means "visit" and has a wide range, including "punish".
b: paqad 'al is literally "visit upon". It means "count", "appoint", "check on", and, with 'al, to bring the consequences of wrongdoing onto someone (Exodus 20:5). Its meaning in this verse (and again in 3:14) is: "I will examine you, and what I find I will deal with". "Punish" is the usual English, but "call to account" keeps the sense of a hearing before a sentence. Because the same verb is used for the altars of Bethel in 3:14, the Plain English Translation uses the same English for both.

p: The verb no'adu can mean "met by appointment" or "agreed".
b: nô'adu is from y'd, "to meet by arrangement" (compare Exodus 25:22; Numbers 17:4, where the LORD "meets" Moses). The Greek has "unless they have made themselves known to each other", reading noda'u. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew. The seven questions of 3:3-6 move from ordinary cause and effect to the city: where a result is seen, a cause is behind it. The Hebrew also does not say that the two are people; the Plain English Translation adds "people".

a: Does a lion roar in the woods
p: A chain of questions that says every event has a cause and then names the prophet's cause.
b: The questions in 3:3-6 each expect "no". Two walk together only if they agreed; a lion roars when it has prey; a bird falls when there is a snare; a trap springs when it has caught something; a ram's horn alarms a city; disaster in a city is the LORD's doing. Verses 7-8 use the same logic for prophecy: if the LORD has spoken, someone must speak. Some think the chain is a defence of Amos against the claim that he had no right to prophesy (7:12-13). Wolff sees an old school of wisdom at work; others call it a plain sermon outline.

a: the LORD has not done it
p: The verse claims the LORD is behind disaster; readers have asked whether that includes moral evil.
b: The Hebrew ra'ah means "harm" or "calamity" and not necessarily "evil" in a moral sense. The question asks whether a city can be struck by disaster without the LORD being behind it. Isaiah 45:7 and Lamentations 3:38 say the same. Most Jewish and Christian readers take it of judgment sent for sin. Many readers take it as a warning that the disaster is deserved, and as a statement against the idea that events come by chance. It does not say that the LORD does evil acts. See also the question of God and evil in the book of Lamentations (Lamentations 3:37-39).

p: The word sod is the private talk of a council.
b: sod is a circle of close friends or advisers, and so "private counsel" (Psalm 25:14; Proverbs 3:32). In the prophets it points to the heavenly council in which the LORD decides and a true prophet stands (Jeremiah 23:18, 22; Job 15:8; 1 Kings 22:19-23). Abraham is told the LORD's plan for Sodom for the same reason (Genesis 18:17). The verse claims that a true prophet has been told by the LORD. Many scholars think 3:7 is a later addition because it interrupts the link between 3:6 and 3:8, and because its wording is like Deuteronomic prose; the Greek has "instruction" (paideia).

t: The lion roars; the prophet speaks
p: The roaring lion from 1:2 returns as the reason for prophecy.
b: The lion's roar links 1:2, 3:4 and 3:8. The LORD roars; people are afraid; and the one who has heard the LORD speak cannot keep silent. The same pair of terms ("fear" and "prophesy") shows up in Jeremiah 20:9, where the word is like a fire in his bones. Amos defends his own mission here: he does not choose to prophesy any more than a person chooses to be afraid when a lion roars. This is the nearest Amos comes to a call story (compare 7:15).

a: two legs or a scrap of an ear
p: A shepherd had to show what was left of a killed animal.
b: The law said that if an animal in his care was torn by a beast, the shepherd must "bring what is left as a witness" (Exodus 22:13), and Jacob mentions it too (Genesis 31:39). Amos turns the proof into a warning: all that will be saved of Samaria's wealth will be a corner of a bed. Commentators divide: the scraps may be proof of the loss, or a sign that a few will survive. The Plain English Translation keeps both possible; the picture is of what is left, not how much.

p: Bethel was the northern kingdom's chief shrine; its altar was the place of refuge.
b: Jeroboam I set up a golden calf at Bethel and Dan (1 Kings 12:28-33); the altar there was the one cursed by the man of God from Judah (1 Kings 13:1-5). Amaziah calls it "the king's sanctuary" (7:13). The horns of an altar were the corners where a person could take hold to be safe (1 Kings 1:50-51). When the horns are cut off and fall, even the place of refuge is gone. The Plain English Translation uses the same "call to account" as in 3:2.

p: Panels of carved ivory decorated the palaces of Samaria.
b: King Ahab built an "ivory house" (1 Kings 22:39), and excavators at Samaria found hundreds of carved ivory plaques from the 9th and 8th centuries, in the style of Phoenician and Syrian work. The winter house and summer house also point to wealth: the poor lived in one-room homes. Amos does not say a house of ivory is wrong; he says the house is built from the poor (3:10) and will be swept away.

p: Bashan was known for fat cattle; the women of Samaria (or its elite) are the cows.
b: Bashan, east of the Sea of Galilee, was famous for fine cattle (Psalm 22:12; Ezekiel 39:18; Deuteronomy 32:14). The Hebrew parot is female ("cows"), and the verbs are feminine plural, so Amos speaks to women: probably the wives of the wealthy, whose demand for drink (4:1) rests on the squeezing of the poor. Some readers think the feminine forms are a general insult for all the leaders, men included (Andersen and Freedman are cautious on the point). The medieval Jewish commentators take the cows as the wives of the princes and officers (Rashi, Radak, Ibn Ezra); the Targum has no cows and addresses "the wealthy of the mountain of Samaria". Whichever way it is read, it is a harsh phrase, and the book kept it. The image has also been used against women in the church; the passage is aimed at wealth and power and not at being female.

p: The captives are pulled out like fish.
b: The words are tsinnot ("hooks", perhaps "thorns" or "barbs") and sirot dugah ("fish hooks"; sir usually means "pot"). Assyrian sculptures show prisoners led by cords or rings through the lip (the picture is also in 2 Kings 19:28, "I will put my hook in your nose"), and Ezekiel 29:4 uses a hook for Pharaoh. The transcription of 4Q78 has a different word where the Masoretic Text has sirot ("hooks"): it reads sopod before "fish", a word no one can identify, so it gives no help with the sense. The sense is "dragged off like fish". 4:3 continues with women leaving through breaches in the wall.

p: A call in the shape of a priest's invitation, turned around.
b: The verse imitates the call to worship: "Come to the sanctuary" (Psalm 95:6; Psalm 100:2). The priests' call to worship is changed into a call to rebellion (pesha', the word used in 1:3). The Hebrew is often read as sarcasm: go ahead, bring your offerings, you are only making your rebellion worse. Bethel and Gilgal were northern shrines (Hosea 4:15; 12:11). Some propose that Amos is quoting the priests' own entrance liturgy and giving it an ironic answer (Wolff, Paul).

t: "Every three days" or "on the third day"?
p: The Hebrew says "for three days".
b: lishloshet yamim is literally "to three days". Options: "every three days" (a pile-up of offerings, mocking the zeal); "on the third day" after arrival; "every third year" is also proposed because Deuteronomy 14:28 and 26:12 give a tithe every third year. The Greek has eis ten triemerian, "for the three-day period", which supports "every three days" better than "on the third day". The Plain English Translation follows the first reading as the mocking one. Nothing in the law asks for a tithe every three days.

a: a thank offering of leavened bread
p: The law allowed leavened loaves with a thank offering but not burned on the altar.
b: A thank offering (todah) came with loaves, some leavened (Leviticus 7:13), but leaven was never to be burned on the altar (Leviticus 2:11; Leviticus 6:17). Amos says "send up in smoke" the leavened bread. Whether Amos is accusing them of breaking the rule, or only mocking their zeal, is unclear: "this is what you love". "Make them heard" refers to the custom of announcing a freewill gift to the crowd (Psalm 66:13-16). The note is not that the offering is wrong but that it is empty.

p: An idiom for having nothing to eat.
b: Clean teeth meant that no food had been between them. The next line explains it: "a shortage of bread". The five disasters of 4:6-11 are the kinds of trouble the covenant curses of Leviticus 26:14-39 and Deuteronomy 28 name: hunger, drought, blight and locusts, plague and war together (4:10), and a destruction like Sodom (Deuteronomy 29:23). Neither chapter lists them in this order. Each of the five is followed by the same line. The pattern shows that Amos's message does not start with new things but with the old threats of the covenant.

a: did not turn back to me
t: The refrain "you did not turn back"
p: Five times the same line closes a disaster.
b: The Hebrew ve-lo shavtem 'adai, "yet you did not return to me", is repeated at 4:6, 8, 9, 10 and 11. shuv is the verb for repentance in the prophets (Hosea 14:1; Jeremiah 3:12; Joel 2:12-13). The Plain English Translation says "turn back", the same as the site's Jeremiah, and keeps it distinct from "return" from exile (9:14, "turn the fortunes ... around"). The LORD's plagues were meant to lead to repentance (1 Kings 8:33-37). They did not, so the final warning is 4:12.

p: In Palestine rain and its failure were the first sign of the LORD's favor.
b: Rain falls from autumn to spring, and a failure before the harvest destroys the crop (Deuteronomy 11:14; 1 Kings 17:1). "Three months before the harvest" means the spring rains that fill the grain. A drought that falls on one city and not the next shows that it is not chance. Rain was given by the LORD, not by Baal (compare 1 Kings 18:1; Hosea 2:8-9).

p: The Hebrew word gazam names one kind of locust.
b: gazam is the "cutting" locust, from the root "to cut off". It is the first of four locust words in Joel 1:4 and also appears in Joel 2:25. The Plain English Translation uses the same English as Joel's, to keep the four words distinct there. Amos 7:1 uses a different word, gobai.

p: The phrase may mean the plagues of Egypt, or a plague coming by the road from Egypt.
b: be-derekh Mitsrayim is literally "in the way of Egypt". Readings: like the plagues of Egypt, especially the disease on the animals (Exodus 9:3-7); "on the road to Egypt", the way an army or a plague came; or "the way Egypt would suffer it". The Plain English Translation takes the first reading. The "capture of horses" is war's loss; the stench of camps, bodies unburied. Plague (dever) was one of the covenant curses (Leviticus 26:25; Deuteronomy 28:21).

t: A stick snatched from the fire
p: The survivors are like a log pulled out of a burning house.
b: Zechariah 3:2 uses the same picture: "Is this not a log snatched from the fire?" (own rendering). The destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:24-25) is the model of total overthrow. Amos says that part of Israel was overthrown "the way God overturned Sodom", and the survivors are only a charred stick, and that gives the next verse its weight. The Plain English Translation keeps "God" in the third person as the Hebrew does, though the LORD is speaking, since "like the overthrow of God" (elohim) may be a Hebrew way to say "a mighty overthrow".

a: get ready to meet your God
p: Is the line a threat, or a call to prepare for a meeting?
b: hikkon liqrat 'eloheikha is the verb used for Israel's preparation at Sinai (Exodus 19:11, 15, 17). Some read a threat: the LORD comes as a judge, with no way of escape (Wolff, Paul). Others read an opening: the verse may be a last call to repent, with the outcome left unspoken. The verse has often been used for funerals and for warnings of death. In its context it is not about death but about God coming to Israel as at Sinai, with the same terror. 4:13 follows with the LORD who makes the mountains.

a: walks on the high places of the earth
p: 4:13, 5:8-9 and 9:5-6 praise the LORD as maker and judge.
b: Three short hymns share the same features: participles ("who forms ... who creates"), the closing line "the LORD ... is his name", and themes of creation and judgment. Crenshaw argued that all three come from one hymn, broken into three and placed to close the sections of judgment. Wolff and Jeremias assign them to later editors; Andersen and Freedman defend them as Amos's. "Treads on the high places of the earth" shows the LORD as master of the mountains (Micah 1:3; Deuteronomy 32:13; Job 9:8) and also of the "high places" (Hebrew bamot, the same word as the shrines).

t: The funeral song for the living
p: Amos sings a qinah over Israel while it is still alive.
b: qinah is the dirge sung at a death (2 Samuel 1:17-27; Jeremiah 9:17-20). The Plain English Translation uses "lament" and the Lamentations term. The meter of a qinah (a long line followed by a short one) cannot be kept in English. Amos sings it while Israel is at its most prosperous; the effect is shock. The poem in 5:2 is only two lines, and 5:3 gives the reason.

p: Betulat Yisrael is a title for the nation as a young woman not yet married.
b: betulat "virgin" is used for a nation as a young woman, as in "the virgin Daughter Zion" (2 Kings 19:21) and "the virgin Israel" (Jeremiah 18:13; 31:4, 21). It is a picture of promise cut short: a young woman fallen on the ground and with no one to help her up. The word "rise" (qum) comes back at 7:2, 5 and 8:14, and in 9:11 the LORD "sets up again" what has fallen.

p: The sums say that ninety percent of the army will not come home.
b: A city that sent a thousand men will have a hundred left; one that sent a hundred will have ten. The numbers are round, as in a stylized report. They match the covenant threat: "You were once as many as the stars in the sky, but only a handful of you will be left" (Deuteronomy 28:62). The Greek of 5:3 is the same. This is the first of Amos's predictions of defeat in war; Assyria is never named in the book, but see 5:27 and 6:14.

p: The call is for the LORD himself, not for a shrine, and the Talmud made it the summary of the commandments.
b: The verb darash is "seek", "consult", "inquire". It is used for going to a shrine or a prophet (1 Samuel 9:9) and for turning to the LORD (Deuteronomy 4:29; Jeremiah 29:13). The Talmud (Makkot 23b-24a) tells how the 613 commandments were reduced: David to eleven (Psalm 15), Isaiah to six, Micah to three, Isaiah again to two, then Amos to one, "Seek me and live", and Habakkuk to one, "the righteous will live by his faith". The story is a rabbinic teaching and not a historical report.

t: A pun on Gilgal and Bethel
p: The Hebrew plays on sounds: Gilgal will gilgal into galut, and Bethel will become Aven.
b: ha-Gilgal galoh yigleh, "Gilgal will surely go into exile", puns on the name Gilgal; the second half puns on Beit-El ("house of God") and aven ("nothing", "wrongdoing"). Hosea gives the new name: Beth-aven, "house of nothing" (Hosea 4:15; 5:8; 10:5, 8). The Greek has "as though not existing". The Plain English Translation keeps "Aven" because the pun with "Beth-aven" belongs to the Twelve. In 1:5 Aven is a valley in Aram.

t: Beersheba: the shrine in the far south
p: Pilgrims from the north crossed into Judah to go to Beersheba.
b: Beersheba was the southern edge of the land and a patriarchal shrine (Genesis 21:33; 26:23-25; 46:1). That northern Israelites went there, across the border (also 8:14), shows how popular these pilgrimages were. Amos forbids all three shrines, Bethel, Gilgal and Beersheba. The prohibition is not on worship but on going to the places, because the LORD cannot be found there: only in justice (5:14-15, 24).

p: Joseph (Ephraim and Manasseh) stands for the northern tribes.
b: Joseph's sons Ephraim and Manasseh were the leading northern tribes, so "Joseph" and "the house of Joseph" name the northern kingdom (5:15; 6:6; also Psalm 78:67; Obadiah 18). This use shows who is being addressed in the oracle. The Plain English Translation uses "Joseph" as the Hebrew does, and "Israel" for the nation when the Hebrew says Israel.

p: la'anah is a bitter herb, and a picture of bitter injustice.
b: la'anah (wormwood, Artemisia) is paired with poison and gall as the taste of a curse (Deuteronomy 29:18; Jeremiah 9:15; 23:15; Lamentations 3:15, 19). To turn justice into wormwood is to turn the court from a place of sweetness to a place of bitterness (6:12). Revelation 8:11 names a star Wormwood. Verse 7 has no verb for a leading "woe" and hangs between 5:6 and 5:8; some think it was moved there.

p: The Hebrew names kimah and kesil are the best-known stars, but the identification is old and not sure.
b: kimah and kesil are both in Job (Job 9:9; 38:31). The old Greek of this verse names no stars (it has "the one who makes all things and changes them"), so it is no witness for the identification. Many translations take them as the Pleiades and Orion (so the Plain English Translation in Job 9:9 and 38:31). Others have proposed Taurus, Sirius, Arcturus or Scorpio. The point of the verse does not depend on which: the One who set the stars also turns morning to darkness. See also 4:13 and 9:5-6 for the hymn.

p: Legal cases were heard in the open space inside the city gate.
b: The elders judged cases in the gateway (Deuteronomy 21:19; 25:7; Ruth 4:1-2; Job 29:7-8). To "set things right at the gate" is to settle a case fairly or to speak for the wronged. Amos 5:10, 12 and 15 all name the gate; the poor were pushed aside there. This is a rare place in the Bible where a public court is shown as a source of injustice (Isaiah 29:21; Proverbs 22:22).

p: The Hebrew mas-bar is rare; it may be a tax or a rent in grain.
b: mas-bar is uncertain. The reading taken here is a share of the poor farmer's grain taken as rent or as a tax. The Greek has "choice gifts". The point is clear: the rich built stone houses and vineyards from what they took. The curse that follows ("you will not live in them") is the same as the covenant curse in Deuteronomy 28:30 and Zephaniah 1:13.

p: The Hebrew kofer usually means a ransom payment.
b: kofer is the ransom paid to avoid a penalty (Exodus 21:30; Numbers 35:31-32). In a gate dispute it is a bribe to skip the penalty or to get a judge to turn aside (1 Samuel 12:3; Proverbs 6:35). The Law forbids a judge to take such a gift (Exodus 23:8; Deuteronomy 16:19). The picture is a court where the rich can buy the verdict.

p: Why does the wise person keep quiet?
b: Views: (1) the wise person is prudent: it is dangerous to speak (compare Ecclesiastes 3:7; Micah 2:3); (2) the wise are silent because they have lost hope; (3) the line is ironic, a quotation of what the powerful say; (4) the line is a later comment by an editor in a time of persecution (Wolff places it with the "wisdom" additions). The verse sits oddly between the call to seek good (5:14-15) and the call to repent. The Hebrew maskil means "one who acts with understanding".

p: A cautious hope: ulay, "perhaps".
b: ulay "perhaps" or "it may be" shows that the LORD cannot be forced (Exodus 32:30; 2 Samuel 16:12; Joel 2:14; Jonah 3:9; Zephaniah 2:3). This is the nearest Amos comes to promising anything before chapter 9. The "remnant of Joseph" is what is left after the defeat of 5:3. Whether Amos expects the remnant to survive, or whether this is an ironic sentence (the hope is not real) is argued; Wolff reads the verse as a real invitation, and others as a late addition. See the topic on the remnant.

a: I will pass through your midst
p: The LORD passes through Israel as he once passed over it.
b: At the first Passover the LORD "passed through" Egypt to strike the firstborn and "passed over" the houses marked with blood (Exodus 12:12, 23). In Amos the LORD passes through Israel, and no mark protects. The same verb 'avar appears in 7:8 and 8:2 ("I will not overlook them any more"), with the meaning "pass by, spare". The Exodus pattern is turned against Israel.

a: Woe to you who long for the day of the LORD
t: The day of the LORD in Amos
p: Amos gives the oldest recorded use of the phrase, and he reverses it.
b: Amos is the earliest prophet whose book uses "the day of the LORD". His hearers long for it, so it was an expected day of the LORD's victory, probably on their enemies (compare the holy war background in Isaiah 13:6; Joel 1:15; Zephaniah 1:14-18). Amos says it is darkness, not light. Views on the background: (1) holy war, the day the LORD fights for Israel (von Rad); (2) a festival, such as the enthronement of the LORD at New Year (Mowinckel); (3) a popular hope of national salvation (Wolff, Paul). Later Jewish and Christian readers have understood the phrase of the end of time, while for Amos the day is near and historical: war, perhaps the Assyrian invasion. See the topic on the day of the LORD.

p: Every escape leads into another danger.
b: The three animals (lion, bear, snake) are dangers in the shepherd's world (1 Samuel 17:34-37; Hosea 13:7-8). A man escapes the lion and meets the bear, and the one who reaches home is bitten by a snake inside the house, where he thought himself safe. The image describes a day with no safe place; compare 9:1-4 where the same idea is stated outright.

p: The LORD says he will not enjoy the smell of the gatherings, the language of sacrifice.
b: lo ariach is "I will not smell", the verb used for the "soothing smell" of the sacrifice that pleases the LORD (Genesis 8:21; Leviticus 26:31: "I will not smell your soothing smells"). The rare noun 'atsarot is the "closing" assemblies at the end of the pilgrim festivals. Isaiah 1:11-17 has a similar attack on sacrifices, and it ends with "Go after justice" (Isaiah 1:17). The prophets are not against the cult as such (compare Hosea 6:6; Micah 6:6-8); they are against worship that is joined to injustice.
orig: לֹא אָרִיחַ (lo ariach), "I will not smell"

p: The word is the same one used in the three pilgrim feasts.
b: chag is the festival that brought pilgrims to the sanctuary: Unleavened Bread, Weeks and Booths (Exodus 23:14-17). Lamentations uses mo'ed (the appointed time) for the same events. Amos uses both chag and 'atsarah (5:21) and the sacrifices (5:22). Isaiah 1:14 uses the other word, mo'ed. See the topic on feasts.

p: The shelem is a sacrificial meal shared with the worshippers.
b: shelem is the offering of which part was eaten by the worshipper (Leviticus 3; Leviticus 7:11-21). The Plain English Translation uses "peace offering", as Leviticus does on this site. The three offerings of verse 22 are the main kinds: the whole-burnt offering, the grain offering and the shared meal. The LORD says he will not accept (ratsah) or look at them. "Fattened animals" are the best animals.

p: Mishpat and tsedaqah are the two words for what the LORD wants.
b: mishpat is "justice": the right decision in a case, the order of a community. tsedaqah is "righteousness": the behavior that fits the relationship, being in the right. The pair appears often (Isaiah 5:7; Isaiah 56:1; Hosea 2:19; Jeremiah 22:3; Psalm 72:1-2). The verb yigal (from galal, "roll") shows flood water that rolls along. The prayer can be read as a demand now, or a prediction of the LORD's justice coming like a flood. Martin Luther King Jr. quoted the verse (in the wording of the American Standard Version) in his speech at the March on Washington, 28 August 1963. Catholic social teaching, the social gospel and liberation theology have used this verse; see the card on the chapter page.

a: a stream that never runs dry
p: Nachal eitan is a stream that flows in every season.
b: A nachal (a wadi) fills in the rains and dries up in summer. 'eitan means "permanent", "unfailing" (Psalm 74:15). The Plain English Translation's Deuteronomy 21:4 has "a valley with a stream that never runs dry" (Deuteronomy 21:4). So the image is of a seasonal channel that becomes a river that never fails: righteousness that does not stop. Compare the "wadi of the Arabah" in 6:14.

a: Was it to me that you brought sacrifices
t: Did Israel offer in the wilderness?
p: The question expects an answer, but which one?
b: Views: (1) "No": there was no sacrificial system in the wilderness (compare Jeremiah 7:22, where the LORD says he gave no command about burnt offerings in the exodus); (2) "Yes, but not to me alone": they brought offerings in the wilderness yet worshipped other gods too (5:26; Ezekiel 20:16, 24); (3) "Yes, but empty": it shows that the LORD wanted loyalty, not sacrifice. The Hebrew is a yes-or-no question (ha-). Acts 7:42 uses the Greek of this verse in Stephen's speech; see the note at 5:27.

p: The names look like Mesopotamian star gods written with the vowels of "abomination".
b: Sikkuth and Kiyyun (sakkut, kewan) are names of Assyrian-Babylonian astral deities, Sakkuth (a title of Ninurta) and Kajamanu, a name of the planet Saturn. The Hebrew vowels may follow the pattern of shiqqutz, "abomination", as scribes did with names of foreign gods. Others read the words as ordinary Hebrew: sukkat "tent" or "booth" of your king, and kiyyun "pedestal" or "image base". The Greek has "the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Rephan". The Damascus Document (CD 7) quotes the verse in a form that differs from the Masoretic Text in more than vowels: the verb is first person ("I will exile") where the Masoretic Text has "you will carry", and the words for "beyond Damascus" are different. It also explains the "booth" as the books of the Law and "Kiyyun" as the books of the prophets (translated in Vermes; the exact wording has not been checked here against an edition, so no line is cited). This is the strongest Hebrew witness to a text other than the Masoretic one, and it matters for the debate over "beyond Damascus" and "beyond Babylon". The Plain English Translation has "your gods" because 'eloheikhem is plural in form; the Greek and Acts have a singular. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew names and explains the debate.

t: Medieval Jewish readings of Sikkuth and Kiyyun
p: The medieval commentators agree these are idols and differ on the words.
b: Rashi says the names are pagan gods whose images the enemy will load on the exiles' necks. Radak and Ibn Ezra say Kiyyun is the planet Saturn (Hebrew Shabbetai), a name known in the language of Ishmael (kayvan). Both also report a reading of sikkuth from haskeit, "listen": the Israelites listened and obeyed an idol. The Plain English Translation follows the first view and keeps the Hebrew names.

p: The Hebrew verb is a waw-perfect, which is usually future, but the Greek makes it past.
b: ve-nesatem is a verb form most often used for the future or for repeated action. Taken with 5:25 (the wilderness) it can mean "you carried" (past, as the Greek and Acts 7:43 have it); taken with 5:27 (exile) it can mean "you will carry" your idols off in the procession. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew form and reads it as a prediction. It is a short sentence with a big effect: the people who "lift up" (nasa') their gods will be "lifted up" in exile.

p: Stephen quotes the passage with "Babylon" in place of "Damascus".
b: The Hebrew has "beyond Damascus"; the Greek of Amos also has "beyond Damascus". Acts 7:42-43 quotes the Greek and reads: "So I will deport you to the far side of Babylon" (Acts 7:43). Stephen's change is deliberate or follows a form of the text now lost. Babylon was where the people of Jerusalem in Stephen's tradition went in exile, and Damascus lay on the road to Assyria. Stephen uses the text to show that Israel was always turning to idols in the wilderness. See the topic on Acts.

p: Amos names both capitals in one woe.
b: The oracle is addressed to the leaders of both kingdoms: those at ease in Zion (Jerusalem) and those trusting the mountain of Samaria. Some scholars think "in Zion" was added by a Judean editor, because the rest of the chapter has only Samaria and Joseph (Wolff); others point to Amos's own Judean background (Paul). The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew. The leaders feel safe because they are the foremost nation, and the whole people comes to them.

p: Three cities that Assyria took, used to ask if Israel is any safer.
b: kalneh is read as the city Calneh (Kullani in Assyrian texts), but the oldest Greek does not read it: it has "cross over, all of you, and see" (diabete pantes kai ide), as if the Hebrew were kullanah, "all of them", and it calls Gath "the strongest of all these kingdoms". The place name is therefore not certain. If Calneh is right, it was taken by Tiglath-pileser III in 738 BC, Hamath by Sargon II in 720 BC, and Gath (Philistine) by Sargon II about 712 BC, in the usual dating. Those events were later than Amos's own time, so many commentators treat 6:2 as a later addition. Others think the verse refers to earlier events, such as a Hamath conquered by Jeroboam II (2 Kings 14:28) or by Aram. Because the reading and the reference are uncertain, the verse is not a safe basis for dating the book. Isaiah 10:9 links Calneh and Hamath the same way.

p: The Hebrew shevet may mean a seat of power.
b: shevet chamas is literally "a seat of violence", from the verb "to sit". They push the day of disaster away in their minds, and in practice they bring violence's seat, or throne, nearer. Some take the "seat" as the court where judges sit, with violence ruling there. The Greek reads shevet as shabbat and has "false sabbaths". The Plain English Translation keeps the picture of a seat.

p: A scene of ease: ivory couches, lamb and calf, and music.
b: Lambs and fattened calves were eaten at feasts, not every day. Ivory beds were found in the style of Phoenician furniture at Samaria and elsewhere. See 3:15. The figures of eating meat, drinking wine in bowls and using the best oils sum up the luxury Amos condemns; it is not that the pleasures are wrong, but the people do not care about the ruin of Joseph.

p: Is the comparison with David a praise or a mockery?
b: David played the lyre and was associated with the Temple musicians (1 Chronicles 23:5; Amos 6:5; Nehemiah 12:36). The Plain English Translation says they "design musical instruments of their own". Views: the comparison mocks their claim to be like David; or it points to David as a king who also loved music but whose music served the LORD. The verb for what the rich do with the harp (para') is rare, and the meanings "improvise", "babble" and "strum" have all been offered.

p: The word marzeach names a kind of banquet club known across the ancient Near East.
b: marzeach appears in Jeremiah 16:5 (a "house of mourning") and in Ugarit, Phoenician and Palmyrene texts, as a banquet of a society, often with wine and tied to the dead. Some think Amos refers to a funeral banquet. The Hebrew is mirzach seruchim, "the marzeach of the sprawled". The Plain English Translation uses "revelry", which is accurate in tone but not in form.

p: Ge'on Ya'aqov can mean the people's arrogance or the LORD himself as their pride.
b: ge'on Ya'aqov is "pride of Jacob" also at 8:7. In Psalm 47:4 it means the good land Israel is proud of; in Nahum 2:2 it may mean the glory the LORD restores. In 8:7 the LORD swears by it. Views: (1) the LORD himself (he swears by his own self in 6:8; Jacob's pride is his God); (2) the arrogance of the nation, which the LORD hates; (3) the land or Zion. The Plain English Translation keeps the two uses of the phrase identical.

a: the one who burns the body
p: The Hebrew describes a man gathering bodies in a plague, possibly to burn them.
b: Israelites usually buried the dead; burning was exceptional (the bodies of Saul and his sons, 1 Samuel 31:12; spices burned for kings, Jeremiah 34:5). The verse describes a house where all have died and the last man goes into the dark of the house to ask if anyone else lives. "Hush!" is spoken so that the LORD's name is not heard, for fear of drawing him near. The Plain English Translation reads the text as it stands; the verse is difficult, and the meaning of "his loved one" (Hebrew dodo, "his uncle" or "his relative") is not sure.

p: Rosh is a bitter plant; la'anah is wormwood.
b: The first noun rosh names a bitter plant that was poisonous (Deuteronomy 29:18; 32:32; Hosea 10:4). With "wormwood" it repeats 5:7: justice turned bitter. The two questions about horses and oxen show something that is not done, and the verse says that the leaders have done the unthinkable. See the entry on the variant for the second question.

p: Both names are puns: "Nothing" and "Horns".
b: Lo-devar sounds like lo davar, "a nothing" (Mephibosheth lived in Lo-debar, 2 Samuel 9:4; 17:27). Qarnayim means "two horns", and horns stand for strength (Deuteronomy 33:17; 1 Kings 22:11). So the leaders boast: "We took Horns by our own strength", but they have taken Nothing. Both towns lay in the Transjordan, probably taken by Jeroboam II (2 Kings 14:25, 28). In Genesis 14:5 Ashteroth-karnaim is an older town. The Plain English Translation keeps the names and the sense is in the pun.

p: Amos never names Assyria here, but the readers know who it is.
b: The LORD "raises up a nation": Assyria, the rising power. The boundaries are chosen on purpose. Jeroboam II "won back Israel's border, from Lebo-hamath to the Sea of the Arabah" (2 Kings 14:25). Amos names the same two points, except he says "the wadi of the Arabah": the oppressor will reach the whole of that new border. The exact wadi is debated; it is often placed at the Wadi el-Hesa, south of the Dead Sea.

p: A locust plague at the time of the late crop would destroy the year's only fodder.
b: The word here is gobai (a locust swarm), not gazam (4:9). The late crop (leqesh) is the spring grass after the winter rains, the fodder that livestock would live on until the dry summer. Locusts coming after the king has taken his share leave nothing for the farmer. The first two visions (locusts, fire) are stopped by the prophet's prayer; the third and fourth are not.

p: The prophet prays for forgiveness before any disaster has happened.
b: selach na is "please forgive". Only God is the subject of this verb in the Bible. The prophet as intercessor appears with Moses (Exodus 32:11-14; Numbers 14:13-19), Samuel (1 Samuel 7:5-9) and Jeremiah (Jeremiah 14:11; and Jeremiah 15:1 where intercession is stopped). Here Amos prays twice and is heard twice. His appeal is not that Israel is innocent but that it is "so small" (qaton), too weak to survive. The root qum, "rise" (5:2), asks how Jacob can stand again.

p: The Hebrew nicham is the same verb for "regret" and "change one's mind"; the visions use it twice.
b: nicham is the verb used when the LORD stops a planned disaster. The site's Plain English Translation has "So the LORD changed his mind about the harm he had said he would do to his people" (Exodus 32:14) and "I will change my mind about the harm I planned to do to it" (Jeremiah 18:8). The same wording is used here. Many English Bibles say "relent"; the same Hebrew verb in Joel 2:13 and Jonah 3:10 is "change his mind" on this site too. The text speaks as if God responded to a prayer; others say Numbers 23:19 and 1 Samuel 15:29 deny that God changes his mind. Jews and Christians have read the tension as human speech about an unchanging God, as real responsiveness, or both. See the topic on God's change of mind and the card on the chapter page. In 7:8 and 8:2 the pattern stops: he will no longer "overlook" Israel.

p: The Hebrew says the LORD "calls for a contention" (rib) by fire.
b: qore' larov ba-esh: the LORD summons a legal dispute (rib) which fire carries out. In the prophets the LORD has a "lawsuit" with Israel (Hosea 4:1; Micah 6:2). The fire dries up "the great deep" (tehom rabbah, the waters under the earth, Genesis 7:11; Amos 9:3 speaks of the sea floor), and would eat the farmland. Some think of a drought or a fiery heat wave. The Greek reads "he called for judgment by fire". The word chelek ("portion") can be the allotted land or the people's share.

a: I am setting a plumb line
p: A rare word, found only in this vision, and its meaning is argued.
b: 'anak occurs only in Amos 7:7-8. Options: a plumb line (a builder's lead weight on a cord, Zechariah 1:16; 2 Kings 21:13 uses a different word for the plumb line, mishqolet); "lead" or "tin" (Akkadian anaku is tin or lead); or "tin" as a metal wall. The Greek has "adamant" (hard metal, steel). The Plain English Translation reads "plumb line" because it fits the test of a wall built true, with the LORD testing Israel against the standard (compare "I will make justice the measuring cord" in Isaiah 28:17, where the Hebrew is qav). The "wall" that is tested may be Israel itself. The one standing "on" the wall ('al) may stand beside it. Verse 8: "I am setting a plumb line in the middle of my people": the test is now public.

a: I will not overlook them any more
t: "I will not pass them by again"
p: The verb avor lo means pass by and not pay attention, so, forgive.
b: 'avor lo is literally "pass by to him": not take notice of the sin (Micah 7:18; Proverbs 19:11; Proverbs 20:3). In 7:8 and 8:2 the LORD says he will no longer do so. The Plain English Translation says "overlook", the way a person overlooks an offence. The same verb is used for the LORD passing through Egypt (Exodus 12:12) and for the LORD "passing through" Israel (5:17).

p: Isaac appears as a name for the people only here (7:9, 16).
b: Amos uses "Isaac" for the nation in 7:9 and 7:16, matching "Jacob" and "Israel", and he does not use "Abraham". The high places were sanctuaries on hills (1 Kings 3:2-3); Beersheba, Isaac's place (Genesis 26:23-25), was a shrine for northerners (5:5; 8:14). The prophecy against "the house of Jeroboam" is what Amaziah reports. In 2 Kings 15:8-12 Jeroboam's son Zechariah was killed by Shallum after six months, which ended Jehu's line, just as 2 Kings 10:30 had promised four generations.

t: Amaziah, priest of the king's sanctuary
p: Amos meets an official priest, who reports him to the king.
b: Amaziah is the chief priest of Bethel (compare Jehoiada at Jerusalem, 2 Kings 12:9; Pashhur, Jeremiah 20:1-2). His report to Jeroboam calls Amos a conspirator (qashar), the word used of coups (2 Kings 15:10, 15). It is a political charge. Nothing in the book says that Amos was arrested or killed; the story stops with a counter-prophecy to Amaziah (7:16-17). The story is in prose; the rest of the book is mostly poetry.

a: Jeroboam will die by the sword
p: Amaziah's report does not match what Amos said in 7:9.
b: Amos said "I will get up against the house of Jeroboam with a sword" (7:9): the dynasty, not the king himself. Amaziah reports that Amos said Jeroboam would die by the sword. 2 Kings 14:29 says only "Jeroboam lay down with his ancestors, with the kings of Israel." Views: (1) Amaziah sharpened Amos's words to make a charge of treason; (2) Amos did say something like this and it did not come true, as with other prophecies not fulfilled in detail; (3) "sword" refers to the dynasty's fall (Zechariah killed, 2 Kings 15:10). The Plain English Translation does not harmonize the texts.

p: Amaziah calls him chozeh, the same word as "he saw" in 1:1.
b: chozeh is a "seer", the title given to Gad (2 Samuel 24:11) and to Jehu son of Hanani (2 Chronicles 19:2); Hanani himself is called ro'eh, a related word for a seer, in 2 Chronicles 16:7. In the mouth of Amaziah it may be a polite title or an insult. "Eat bread there" means "earn your living there": prophets were supported by those who consulted them (1 Samuel 9:7-8; Micah 3:5, 11). Amaziah assumes Amos prophesies for pay and tells him to go home.

a: the king's sanctuary, the temple of the kingdom
p: Bethel was a state shrine.
b: miqdash melekh and bet mamlakah: Bethel belongs to the crown. This is the claim that the king, not the prophet, controls what is said there. Compare Jeroboam I's "high places" (1 Kings 12:31-32). Amos speaks in the sanctuary against the state, and the priest's reply is that the state decides who speaks.

t: "I am no prophet" or "I was no prophet"?
p: The verbless Hebrew can be present or past; the choice changes what Amos denies.
b: The Hebrew is lo navi 'anokhi ve-lo ben-navi 'anokhi, with no verb "to be". Reading as present, "I am no prophet", Amos refuses the label that Amaziah gives: he is not a professional prophet, a member of a prophetic guild (ben navi, "son of a prophet", as in 2 Kings 2:3-5), but a herdsman whom the LORD sent (so Wolff and Paul). Reading as past, "I was no prophet" (the Greek has "I was", ēmēn), he says he was a herdsman before the LORD called him and is a prophet now by the LORD's order (so many older commentators; Jerome's Latin has "I am not a prophet", non sum). Zechariah 13:5 has the same verbless pattern for a false prophet who denies his role. The grammar does not decide: a clause without a verb has no present marker either. The Plain English Translation follows the present because that is the reading most commentators choose today and because it suits Amos's reply to a charge of prophesying for pay. The connective ki before "a herdsman I" is itself part of the debate ("but rather" favors the present, "for" favors the past), and the Plain English Translation leaves it unwritten. Each reading is argued by good scholars; the medieval Jewish readings are in the next note.

t: Medieval Jewish readings of "I am no prophet"
p: The commentators divide on the tense and agree that Amos denies being a paid prophet.
b: Radak ("I was not a prophet from my youth, nor a prophet's son who taught me the ways of prophecy") and Ibn Ezra ("I was not a prophet of the LORD") read the verse as past. Rashi writes "I am not one of your false prophets, who take pay", and says Amos did not need the money: he was a wealthy owner of cattle and property. He is following the Targum, which has "for I am an owner of cattle, and I have sycamores in the plain". For Rashi the issue is pay; for Radak and Ibn Ezra it is Amos's earlier life.

p: The boles shiqmim cut or pinched the figs so that they would ripen.
b: The sycamore fig (Ficus sycomorus) bears fruit that needs to be nicked or pinched for it to ripen; the work was done by a boles. The tree does not grow in the cold hill country of Tekoa; it grows in the warm Jordan valley and the coastal plain (1 Kings 10:27; 1 Chronicles 27:28). So Amos either worked in the lowlands or his work took him there. boqer "herdsman" is a keeper of cattle (not sheep). Both tasks suggest a man of some means, not a village poor man; this is argued (Hayes).

a: took me from walking behind the flock
t: "The LORD took me from the flock"
p: Like David, a shepherd is taken by the LORD for a new task.
b: The wording matches the story of David: "It was I who took you off the grazing land, from walking behind the flock" (2 Samuel 7:8). Amos has no vision of the throne like Isaiah 6 and no call like Jeremiah 1. His call is only this one sentence and the command "Go, prophesy". 3:8 says the same: "The Lord GOD has spoken. Who will not prophesy?"

p: The Hebrew natap means "drip", and refers to speaking.
b: hittif is "drip", a word for prophetic speech, sometimes with an edge of contempt (Micah 2:6, 11; Ezekiel 21:2). Amaziah repeats Micah's opponents: "Do not drip words". The Plain English Translation says "rant". For Amaziah a prophet is like a man who rambles on.

a: will become a prostitute in the city
p: Amos answers Amaziah with a personal sentence.
b: The fate is the fate of a captured city: wife taken by soldiers, children killed, land shared out by the conquerors and the priest dead "on unclean ground" (a foreign land, Hosea 9:3; Ezekiel 4:13). A priest was to avoid uncleanness; to die in an unclean land would be the end of everything he stood for. The sentence ends with the refrain: Israel will go into exile "away from its land", the sentence that Amaziah quoted in 7:11.

p: The Hebrew words for summer fruit and for end sound almost the same.
b: qayits "summer fruit" and qets "end" differ by one vowel sound. The fruit, picked at the end of the season, is ripe, and so is Israel. English cannot keep the pun; the Plain English Translation gives both words. A tenth-century inscription from Gezer, the "Gezer calendar", has a month "of summer fruit" in its list of farm seasons, which shows that the word was in common farm use.

p: Ezekiel repeats the phrase in his own announcements.
b: Ezekiel 7:2-6 repeats "the end" (qets) four or five times for Judah, using Amos's word. The Flood story uses a different word (Genesis 6:13: "The end of all flesh is coming before me"). The "end" is for "my people Israel": the LORD says "my people" even as he ends them.

p: Is the Hebrew heikhal a temple or a palace, and is shirot "songs"?
b: heikhal can be a palace (Psalm 45:8, 15) or a temple. shirot is "songs", but the Greek took the word as shorot, "ceiling beams", and reads: "the ceiling panels of the temple will wail" (compare 1 Kings 6:15). The Plain English Translation reads "songs". "Hush!" (has) is the cry for silence before the LORD (Habakkuk 2:20; Zephaniah 1:7) or a command to the survivors to be quiet (6:10).

p: The written text and the reading tradition differ by one letter.
b: The Ketiv (the written form) and the Qere (the form to be read) differ in the second word: the Ketiv is 'anwei "the humble" and the Qere is 'aniyyei "the afflicted". The words are close in sense and the Plain English Translation has "poor", which follows the Qere. The same list of the poor and needy appears in 2:6-7; 4:1; 5:11-12. For the poor as a group in the prophets, see the topic on poverty.

t: New Moon and Sabbath: work stopped
p: Both days were days of rest, and the merchants wanted them over.
b: On the New Moon (2 Kings 4:23; Isaiah 1:13) and the Sabbath, normal trade stopped. Amos shows the traders impatient to open their grain stores. It shows the Sabbath was kept as a rest from trade in Amos's day; the later parallel is Nehemiah 13:15-22. The commandment is in Exodus 20:8-11 and Deuteronomy 5:12-15. Note that the traders keep the day, but they hate it.

a: the ephah small and the shekel large
p: They shrink the measure and raise the weight.
b: The ephah is a dry measure (about 22 liters) and the shekel is a weight of silver (about 11 grams). A merchant who sold grain by a small ephah and took payment by a heavy shekel gets more silver for less grain. "Scales that lie" (moznei mirmah) completes the picture. The law forbade all this (Leviticus 19:35-36; Deuteronomy 25:13-16); see Proverbs 11:1 and Micah 6:10-11.

p: Even the floor sweepings were sold as grain.
b: mappal bar is the waste of the wheat, the chaff and bad grain swept up. Selling it as food is another fraud, perhaps meant for the poor who could only buy that. The verse also repeats the buying of the poor for silver and sandals (2:6); compare the note there on debt slavery.

p: Amos compares the shaking of the earth to the Nile's yearly flood.
b: ye'or is the Egyptian word for the Nile (Genesis 41:1; Exodus 7:15). Its rise and fall each year was well known. The earth shakes, rises and falls like the Nile: an earthquake picture (compare 1:1). The Masoretic text of the first word is ka'or, "like the light"; the Plain English Translation reads it as ka-ye'or, "like the Nile", as 9:5 and the next line do (see the variant), and the Greek has "like a river". A written form in the Hebrew text (Ketiv) reads "will be watered" for "sink", and the Qere reads "sink"; the Plain English Translation follows the Qere. The same lines are in 9:5.

a: make the sun set at midday
p: Amos describes a sun going dark at noon; readers have asked if he saw an eclipse.
b: The Assyrian eponym records mention a solar eclipse in the month Simanu of 763 BC, in the reign of Ashur-dan III. Some think Amos has in mind such an event or one like it; others see a poetic picture of the day of the LORD (5:18-20; Joel 2:10, 31). In Matthew's gospel: "From the sixth hour until the ninth hour, darkness lay over the whole land" (Matthew 27:45). Christian readers since early times have linked the verse with the darkness at the crucifixion; Matthew does not quote Amos, so the link is an echo drawn by readers. See Jeremiah 15:9 for a similar picture.

p: The worst grief that a parent can know.
b: An only child was the symbol of the worst loss (Jeremiah 6:26; Zechariah 12:10; Genesis 22:2). The line says that the festivals will turn to mourning and the entire land will be like a house where the only child has died. Sackcloth and baldness are signs of mourning (Isaiah 15:2-3; Micah 1:16).

a: hearing the words of the LORD
p: The worst famine is silence from God.
b: The LORD sends a famine of his own word. Earlier, "The LORD's word was rare in those days" (1 Samuel 3:1). Micah 3:6-7 and Lamentations 2:9 speak of prophets without visions. The ones who told Amos to stop prophesying (2:12; 7:12-13) will get what they asked for. Deuteronomy 8:3 (quoted in Matthew 4:4) says people live "by every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD". Readers have asked whether this is a time in history (the long silence after the prophets, or the exile) or a condition of the heart. See the topic on the word of God.

p: The Hebrew gives a wide area: from the Dead Sea to the Mediterranean, or the whole world.
b: "From sea to sea, from north to east" names the extent of the search. It may be the Dead Sea to the Mediterranean, or the Mediterranean to the Persian Gulf; the phrase is general (Psalm 72:8; Zechariah 9:10). The people will wander, looking, because the word has gone.

p: The oaths name the northern and southern shrines.
b: Dan, the northernmost shrine of the golden calf (1 Kings 12:29-30), and Beersheba, the southernmost, mark the extent of the land. People swear "by the life of" these. "By the guilt of Samaria" is an ironic oath, since the oath names something the LORD hates. The Greek has "by the propitiation of Samaria". Some scholars read the Hebrew 'ashmat as the name of a god, Ashimah of Hamath who was worshipped in Samaria (2 Kings 17:30). See the entries on the variants.

p: The Lord stands "over" or "beside" the altar, and the altar is not named.
b: Views: (1) the altar at Bethel (3:14; 7:13), with the sanctuary the LORD will strike; (2) the altar in Jerusalem, so that the LORD attacks his own temple (1 Kings 13:1-2 is a similar scene); (3) a scene not tied to a place. The LORD is in the shrine, not as a guest but as the judge who orders the roof to fall. The "capitals" and "thresholds" are parts of a building. The Plain English Translation says "over", the Hebrew 'al can also be "beside" or "upon".

p: Sheol, heaven, Carmel and the sea floor: the LORD is everywhere.
b: The list in 9:2-4 (the world of the dead, the heavens, the top of Carmel, the bottom of the sea, captivity) matches Psalm 139:7-12 and Job 11:8-9. In the psalm the thought brings comfort; in Amos it is a threat. Jonah ran toward the sea (Jonah 1:3). Obadiah 4 also speaks of falling from the height. See the topic on Sheol.

p: The LORD commands a snake in the deep.
b: A serpent in the sea may be the sea monster that the LORD rules (Isaiah 27:1; Job 26:13; Psalm 74:13-14). Some link it to Leviathan. The Plain English Translation says "serpent" because the Hebrew has nachash, the same word as for the snake in 5:19 and Genesis 3. The point is that the sea bottom, the home of chaos in ancient thought, is no refuge.

p: The words are rare; the sense is of God's house in the sky.
b: ma'alot may be "steps" or "upper rooms" (Psalm 104:3 has "upper rooms" for a related noun, aliyyah). 'agudah is "a bundle" (Exodus 12:22 hyssop) or "vault", a dome fixed on earth. The Qere and the Ketiv differ in the suffix. The picture is of a house with a stair going from earth up to heaven, the LORD at the top. The doxology repeats the lines of 5:8.

t: "Are you not like the Cushites to me?"
p: The LORD names Israel beside the people at the edge of the known world and the enemy Philistines and Arameans.
b: Cush is the land south of Egypt (Nubia), and its people were far away and dark-skinned (Jeremiah 13:23). Amos says the LORD cares for them as much as for Israel. The verse says that the exodus is not unique: the LORD also led the Philistines from Caphtor (Crete or the Aegean, Deuteronomy 2:23; Jeremiah 47:4) and the Arameans from Kir (compare 1:5). It does not deny Israel's election (3:2) but denies that Israel's election means that the LORD is Israel's alone. Views: this makes Israel one nation among others (Wolff, Paul); it is a rhetorical shock, not a new doctrine (Andersen and Freedman); the verse broadens the exodus to a pattern of divine guiding of all peoples (Jewish and Christian universalist readings). The verse has also been misused to claim that Cush is inferior; the Hebrew says the opposite. See the topics on election and Cush.

p: Two places of origin for the Philistines and the Arameans.
b: Caphtor is usually Crete or the Aegean (Jeremiah 47:4; Deuteronomy 2:23), and the Philistines are linked to the Sea Peoples who settled the coast around 1175 BC. Kir is the place of origin of the Arameans (compare 1:5), and Isaiah 22:6 names it with Elam. Its location is unknown, perhaps in Mesopotamia. Amos is the only prophet who gives Kir as the Arameans' former home.

a: will not wipe out the house of Jacob completely
p: The sinful kingdom is wiped out; the house of Jacob is not wiped out completely.
b: Two things are said about Israel in the same verse: the kingdom (a political state) is destroyed, but the house of Jacob (the people) is not completely destroyed. Wolff thinks this verse softens the harsh end of 9:1-4 and is a later addition; Paul and others defend it as Amos's. Jeremiah 30:11 and 46:28 repeat the idea. The remnant doctrine is built from verses like this (topic: remnant).

p: A sieve keeps the stones and lets out the dust, or the other way.
b: A sieve shakes out the dust and keeps the grain. In Amos 9:9 the people are shaken among the nations, and "not one pebble" (tseror, a small stone, or a grain) falls to the ground: nothing of value is lost. The sinners in 9:10 are those who die by the sword. Jesus's words to Peter, "Satan has asked to have all of you, to shake you in a sieve like wheat" (Luke 22:31), use a similar picture of sifting.

a: Disaster will not come near us
p: The sinners say that disaster will not touch them.
b: Other prophets quote this same false comfort: "No harm will come to us" (Jeremiah 5:12), "Is the LORD not in the middle of us?" (Micah 3:11). The people of 5:18 who long for the day of the LORD are the same people who say this.

p: The Davidic house is a hut that has fallen.
b: sukkat David ha-nofelet is a ramshackle hut, not a palace: the dynasty after its collapse. Readings: the Davidic dynasty after the exile (Wolff, Jeremias, who place it after 586 BC); the united kingdom of David before the split (with the hope of reunion, Hosea 3:5; Ezekiel 37:15-28); or the city of Jerusalem. In Jewish tradition the Messiah is called Bar Nafle, "son of the fallen", from this verse (Sanhedrin 96b-97a). The Dead Sea Scrolls use it twice: the Damascus Document (CD 7) explains the "booth of the king" of Amos 5:26-27 as the books of the Law and quotes 9:11 nearby, and 4QFlorilegium (4Q174) reads "the booth of David that is fallen" of the Branch of David (reported in Vermes). The Targum Jonathan reads the booth as the kingdom of the house of David; Rashi quotes it, and Radak reads the booth as David's kingdom too, a figure because a booth shelters the people, raised on the day of redemption. Acts 15:16 quotes it: "build again the fallen tent of David" (Acts 15:16). Christians have read it as fulfilled in the resurrection of Jesus and the church (Acts 15) or as still to come (dispensational readings).

a: over whom my name has been called
p: Belonging: the nations over whom the LORD's name is named.
b: "My name has been called over them" means they belong to the LORD, as a field belongs to its owner after it is named (2 Samuel 12:28; Isaiah 4:1; Deuteronomy 28:10). Acts 15:17 quotes the same words: "all the nations over whom my name has been called" (Acts 15:17). James uses this phrase for the Gentiles who turn to God. In the Hebrew, these "nations" may be the nations once ruled by David's empire (Edom, Moab, Ammon). In the Greek the phrase continues the sentence about all humankind seeking the Lord. Bauckham argues that James's case depends on the phrase "called by my name" as much as on the verb. Rashi, Radak and Ibn Ezra read the Hebrew verse as turned around: Israel, over whom the LORD's name is called, will possess the remnant of Edom and the nations. Radak names the nations David subdued (Edom, Philistia, Moab, Ammon) and says Israel will inherit their land again.

a: will catch up with the reaper
p: The plowing starts before the last harvest is done.
b: Leviticus 26:5 promises, "Your threshing will last until the grape harvest, and the grape harvest until sowing time": a covenant blessing. Amos reverses the curses of 5:11. The Hebrew words for "the mountains drip sweet wine" are shared with Joel 3:18, but the verbs differ (Amos has the causative, "make drip", Joel the simple "drip") and the second clause differs ("all the hills will flow" in Amos, "milk will run down the hills" in Joel), so the Plain English Translation does not make the two verses identical as it does for Amos 1:2 and Joel 3:16. Radak notes that the word "milk" is left to be supplied in Amos, and cites Joel. Whether the two prophets quote each other or share a stock phrase is debated. The vision of abundance is a picture of Eden restored (compare Isaiah 25:6; Isaiah 65:21-23).

a: turn the fortunes of my people Israel around
p: Shuv shevut means to restore a state of life.
b: shuv shevut (or shevit) is "to turn the fortunes". The site's Plain English Translation of Jeremiah has "when I will turn the fortunes of my people Israel and Judah around" (Jeremiah 30:3). The Greek has "I will turn back the captivity", reading shevut as "captivity", and many English Bibles follow it. Both senses fit; the verb is also used where there was no exile (Job 42:10; Hosea 6:11). The Plain English Translation does not decide whether Amos speaks of exile in 9:14.

a: never again will they be torn up
t: The end of the book: hope or addition?
p: Was the promise of 9:11-15 spoken by Amos?
b: Critical scholars (Wolff, Jeremias and many others) say 9:11-15 comes from the time of the exile or after because it assumes a fallen dynasty, and the book's last word until then was judgment (9:8-10). Others argue that Amos could have ended on hope (Hayes, Andersen and Freedman, Paul). Jewish tradition reads it of the return and the Messiah; Christian traditions read it as fulfilled in Christ and the church (Acts 15) or as still to come for Israel; dispensational readings expect a return of Israel to the land (Walvoord, Ryrie); amillennial ones read the land as heaven or the new creation (Hoekema). The text itself says "I will plant them", the language of Jeremiah 24:6 and 32:41. See the card at 9:11-12.
